content: Measles is a significant cause of illness and death among children, particularly in areas where vitamin A deficiency is prevalent. Vitamin A deficiency is recognized as a risk factor for severe measles infections. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends administering a daily oral dose of vitamin A for two consecutive days to children with measles in regions where vitamin A deficiency is common. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether administering vitamin A after a diagnosis of measles reduces mortality, pneumonia, or other complications in children. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to February 2011. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving children with measles who were treated with either vitamin A or a placebo, in addition to standard care. The data from these studies were independently assessed by two reviewers. Dichotomous outcomes were analyzed and expressed as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Subgroup analyses were performed based on factors such as vitamin A dose, formulation, age, hospitalization status, and pneumonia-specific mortality. For continuous outcomes, mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs were calculated. A total of eight trials, involving 2,574 participants, met the inclusion criteria. When all studies were pooled, there was no significant reduction in overall mortality in the group receiving vitamin A (RR 0.70; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.15). The evidence indicated that a single dose of vitamin A did not significantly reduce the risk of mortality. However, administering two doses of vitamin A (200,000 international units (IUs) on consecutive days) was associated with a significant reduction in mortality among children under two years of age (RR 0.21; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.66). Additionally, two doses of vitamin A reduced pneumonia-specific mortality (RR 0.57; 95% CI 0.24 to 1.37), although the confidence interval suggests some uncertainty in this finding. Two doses of vitamin A also significantly reduced the incidence of croup (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.29 to 0.89). However, there was no significant reduction in pneumonia morbidity (RR 0.92; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.22) or diarrhea morbidity (RR 0.80; 95% CI 0.27 to 2.34). Importantly, none of the studies included in this review reported any adverse effects associated with vitamin A administration. In conclusion, the review found no overall significant reduction in mortality with vitamin A therapy for children with measles. However, two doses of vitamin A were effective in reducing overall mortality and pneumonia-specific mortality in children under two years of age. The studies did not directly compare the effects of a single dose versus two doses of vitamin A.
